title: Will AI Be Accessible?
author: Jane Ribadeneyra · Angela Tripp · Molly McDonough

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s public-centred, comparative assessment of court AI by grounding potential benefits and risks in existing access constraints. It particularly reinforces the synthesis on unequal access, insufficient institutional vetting, human verification and oversight, while treating claimed quality gaps as concerns rather than measured findings.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition that direct AI access can shift reliability risks onto self-represented and low-income users while advantaging well-resourced firms. It also endorses managed adoption through acceptable-use policies and safe incorporation rather than blanket avoidance, while noting practical difficulties with disclosure when AI is embedded in existing tools.
qs: I mean, the big firms can purchase the AI software that is specifically trained on legal information and legal knowledge and has fewer hallucinations, whereas self-represented litigants will be using Bing and not have that same quality and have more, you know, a better chance of running into the fake case problem.
And you need to start identifying how to incorporate it and what are the ways you can safely incorporate it.

st.t: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s access-to-justice framing and its cautious distinction between growing practical activity and proven gains. It presents AI as a means to make legal services more accessible and providers more effective, while describing exploratory grant-supported development and testing rather than demonstrated improvements in access or legal outcomes.
qs: Today, I'm speaking with two guests who are closely tracking emerging technology, including generative AI and how these new technologies can be used to make legal services more accessible and providers more effective.
The TIG program supports projects that develop, test, and replicate innovative technologies to increase access to high-quality legal services, the judicial system, and legal information.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s implementation-focused argument by emphasizing that rapid technological change requires adaptable planning and flexible projects. Its support is narrow: it offers practical guidance rather than evidence that AI improves access to justice or service outcomes.
qs: I think you have to put yourself in a position to accept change easily and to be really flexible about the ideas and projects that you're working on.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s cautious, governance-led approach: AI use is likely to spread, but organisations should manage it through acceptable-use policies, safe incorporation and attention to client risks. Its reference to nonexistent cited cases also supports the need for verification, though it provides little evidence on productivity, workforce effects or competence development.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI may improve legal-aid services but uptake alone cannot close justice gaps. It stresses that unequal purchasing power may widen disparities and that safe, meaningful deployment requires human oversight, verification and deliberately bounded uses rather than reliance on autonomous systems.

And so that's always front and center when thinking about the risks of AI, because it's, you know, that was more algorithm than AI, but the problem was the lack of human counterparts and checks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source strongly supports selective, human-led deployment. It identifies bounded access-to-justice uses, distinguishes promising tasks from immature ones, and stresses verification, controlled data, acceptable-use policies, equitable access and deliberate governance rather than broad autonomous reliance.

kp.k: Pandemic accelerated justice-sector technology acceptance, unevenly
kp.d: Ribadeneyra reports that the pandemic produced the substantial shift in technology acceptance previously anticipated, including remote hearings and legal aid delivery. She cautions that some jurisdictions are retreating from remote hearings after the return to in-person activity. Tripp likewise reports increased acceptance among courts and litigants, citing Michigan text reminders and e-filing, while characterizing lawyers as slower to embrace change. These are practitioner observations rather than measured adoption findings.
qs: there are some courts and jurisdictions that are continuing to innovate and introduce new technologies, and there's others that may be stepping back a little bit
I think lawyers are always kind of the slowest to embrace change.
as a state, we're moving forward rapidly now with e-filing, and courts want self-represented litigants to use e-filing as well.

kp.k: Legal aid AI discussions shift toward practical deployment
kp.d: Tripp describes a move from theoretical to practical AI discussions in the preceding several months, with greater interest but unresolved concerns about privacy, bias and due process. Ribadeneyra reports earlier TIG experimentation with chatbots and a Florida intake project funded four years previously to identify legal issues from uploaded documents; the latter found the technology insufficiently mature. She contrasts that experience with rapid contemporary development, without reporting validated performance results.
qs: in the last several months, it's gone from more theoretical conversations to more practical conversations.
The concerns are still great primarily around bias and privacy

We've funded a project four years ago in Florida that would allow applicants to upload certain documents as part of an online intake system and then try and use artificial intelligence to analyze information from those documents to see if they could sort of issue spot what the applicant's legal issues were.
The technology wasn't there yet.

kp.k: Embedded AI creates policy and disclosure difficulties
kp.d: Ribadeneyra argues that AI's integration into everyday software makes acceptable-use policies necessary because people will use it whether organizations know or not. McDonough raises reported fabricated-case incidents and judicial AI affidavits or disclosure requirements; Ribadeneyra responds that users may not know their tools contain AI, complicating such affidavits. The discussion does not identify particular judicial orders or establish a governing disclosure rule.
qs: people are starting to draft acceptable use policies for artificial intelligence because it's, it's coming, you know, people are going to be using it whether you know it or not.
it might be hard for someone to be able to do an affidavit if they don't even necessarily understand that there's AI built into some of the tools that they're using.
they need to update those and address them for acceptable use policies for artificial intelligence

kp.k: Unequal AI purchasing power could widen justice disparities
kp.d: Ribadeneyra predicts that well-resourced large firms will adopt AI more readily than organizations assisting low-income people, increasing the digital divide. Tripp argues that large firms can buy legally trained software with fewer hallucinations while self-represented litigants may rely on Bing and face fabricated-case risks. This is a comparative concern expressed by the speakers, not a measured comparison of tool accuracy.
qs: It's just going to increase that divide between the haves and the have-nots, too.
the big firms can purchase the AI software that is specifically trained on legal information and legal knowledge and has fewer hallucinations, whereas self-represented litigants will be using Bing
And it could do more harm than good in that environment.

kp.k: Chatbots support legal information navigation and human handoffs
kp.d: Ribadeneyra cites Maine's Moose chatbot, a Colorado consumer-debt tool developed with LawDroid, and court chatbot and kiosk systems as existing navigation aids. She proposes combining chatbot interactions with live assistance when needed. Tripp describes Renter Revention as drawing only on website information and considers a similar approach for Michigan Legal Help to improve findability and comprehension; she does not report user-outcome evidence.

There was a chatbot in Colorado that worked with a company called LawDroid to develop a tool to help guide people to consumer debt issues.

Renter Revention is doing, which is a chatbot that feeds only on the information on the website

kp.k: Michigan combines narrow classification with lawyer-reviewed AI drafting
kp.d: Tripp reports that Michigan Legal Help's May 1st launch incorporated Suffolk Law School Lit Lab's Spot AI to classify visitors' problems into top-level legal categories. Separately, staff attorneys already use AI for first drafts and plain-language improvements. She endorses this as assistance to lawyers, conditional on thorough review, editing and checking, rather than direct reliance on unverified output.
qs: We launched it on May 1st.
we incorporated Spot AI, which was one of the tools that are used by several legal aid websites and developed by Suffolk Law School's Lit Lab.
helps people identify of our top level categories which is their legal problem likely.

kp.k: Proposed integrations target routine advocate workflows
kp.d: Ribadeneyra describes a TIG application under review to add AI to a commonly used case management system for case summaries, pro bono recruitment postings and legal issue identification. These are proposed uses integrated into advocates' daily tools, not completed deployments or demonstrated productivity gains.
qs: One of the proposals is to add artificial intelligence to a commonly used case management system, so that the advocates could use it to write a quick case summary, you know, or help them post a case for pro bono recruitment, or help them identify legal issues.
it's maybe something integrated into the tools that advocates are using every day.

kp.k: AI might extend self-help beyond standardized court forms
kp.d: Ribadeneyra and Tripp suggest AI could assist litigants with narrative text in filings. Tripp is uncertain about its contribution to document assembly where prescribed forms remain necessary, but sees potential for matters without forms, such as appealing food-stamp denials from an agency to court. Michigan Legal Help has not automated those matters because narrative and possible briefing requirements make them difficult for self-represented litigants; she explicitly qualifies whether AI could fully address them.
qs: document assembly in general, it's hard for me to comprehend how AI could help with that as long as there are still like required court forms.
places where people need to write a narrative, or as you said, a longer answer, it could be, it could be very helpful.

kp.d: Ribadeneyra identifies an unmet need after brief advice: clients may struggle to complete multistep processes when legal aid cannot take their cases. kp.k: TIG supports shared, replicable experimentation rather than guaranteed success
kp.d: Ribadeneyra describes TIG's annual appropriation of about $4.5 million, $5 million for discrete technology experiments with direct-service legal aid organizations. The program accepts that projects may fail and prioritizes replication and shared learning across organizations. This funding description concerns technology experimentation generally, not an exclusively AI budget.

We understand not everything is going to be a success

kp.k: Automated public decisions risk bias and unchecked harm
kp.d: Tripp warns that courts and agencies may prioritize speed and efficiency while deploying poorly understood or inadequately vetted tools without human oversight. She cites Michigan unemployment-agency automated fraud determinations as a historical example of harm, expressly characterizing that system as more algorithm than AI. Her concern about future AI deployment is grounded in that analogy, not a reported study of generative AI adjudication.
qs: it's courts and agencies using tools that they don't fully understand or haven't thoroughly vetted.
I worry that people will trust the AI too much, put too much faith in it, and skip those important verification, evaluation, assessment steps.
in Michigan, we're still feeling the reverberations from the automated fraud determinations that were issued by the unemployment agency many years ago.
that was more algorithm than AI, but the problem was the lack of human counterparts and checks.

kp.k: Trusted legal content offers a bounded development pathway
kp.d: Ribadeneyra favors plain-language assistance over current legal research uses and proposes training a large language model on reliable statewide legal aid website content. McDonough suggests a bounded dataset could help but explicitly acknowledges residual hallucination potential. The conversation presents this as a development possibility, not proof that restricting source material ensures correct outputs.

Could we train a large language model on that content and deliver it to people using that type of reliable information that could be helpful and know that this is a correct resource for them to have?

kp.k: Equitable deployment requires funding, education and participatory safeguards
kp.d: Ribadeneyra calls for other funders to collaborate with LSC so access to AI is more equitable. Tripp recommends widespread education, use guidelines, algorithm and data transparency, and some governmental regulation. She urges courts and agencies to include litigants, advocates, legal aid and end users when designing AI decision tools, to identify bias before harm occurs. These are recommendations, not existing standards or enacted requirements.
qs: I'd like to see some other funders who could maybe collaborate with the Legal Services Corporation to identify how can we find the resources so that there is equitable distribution and use of these technologies moving forward.
my wish list would include general widespread education and guidelines for use.
More demand for more transparency in algorithms and what data is being used in algorithms.
I do think some governmental scale regulation would probably be good.
solicit, gather and use input from advocates, legal aid folks, end users
To do that on the front end rather than waiting to do something terrible and get sued.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Angela Tripp and Jane Ribadeneyra describe AI as moving from theoretical discussion to practical adoption in legal aid, including through tools organisations already use.
pts.d: Tripp reports increased practical interest in the months preceding the 2023 conversation, while emphasising continuing concerns about bias, privacy and due process. Ribadeneyra says AI is being embedded in existing technology, sometimes without users realising it, and expects adoption whether or not organisations explicitly authorise it. She identifies acceptable-use policies and risk assessment as necessary responses. These are professional observations and near-term expectations, not quantified adoption findings.

pts.k: Ribadeneyra and Tripp predict that unequal access to AI could widen the divide between well-resourced firms and people seeking low-income legal assistance.
pts.d: Ribadeneyra expects larger firms to be better able to integrate and exploit AI than organisations helping low-income people. Tripp adds that firms can purchase legally specialised software that she describes as having fewer hallucinations, whereas self-represented litigants may rely on general-purpose tools such as Bing and encounter fabricated cases. This is a comparative market-access and quality-risk prediction; the speakers supply no pricing evidence or comparative error-rate measurements.

pts.k: Ribadeneyra and Tripp identify AI-assisted navigation and issue classification as ways to help self-represented litigants find and understand legal information.
pts.d: Ribadeneyra cites existing legal-aid and court chatbots, including Maine's Moose, a Colorado consumer-debt tool developed with LawDroid, and court kiosks or avatars in Florida and Maine. She describes a possible pathway from chatbot assistance to a live human interface. Tripp reports that Michigan Legal Help has integrated Suffolk Law School Lit Lab's Spot AI to identify broad legal-problem categories. She also points to Renter Revention's website-content chatbot as a model she is considering for making Michigan Legal Help content easier to find and understand. The examples span earlier chatbot technology and newer AI; they are not presented as equivalent generative-AI systems or as measured outcome improvements.

pts.k: Tripp reports current use of AI for first drafts and plain-language editing, with lawyers retaining responsibility for checking and revising the output.
pts.d: Tripp says Michigan Legal Help staff attorneys already use AI in producing website content. She endorses drafting assistance followed by thorough review, editing and checking, rather than direct reliance on generated content. Ribadeneyra similarly describes plain-language conversion as a good current use, but considers legal research not yet ready. Ribadeneyra also describes a grant proposal—not a completed deployment—to integrate case summaries, pro bono recruitment posts and issue identification into a commonly used case-management system.

pts.k: Tripp sees potential for AI to assist litigants with narrative writing and eventually with matters that lack standard court forms, while explicitly qualifying that potential.
pts.d: Responding to Ribadeneyra's suggestion about drafting longer form responses, Tripp says AI could help users articulate their issues. She distinguishes this from document assembly constrained by required court forms, where she is unsure how AI would help. Her longer-term example is an appeal from an agency's denial of food stamps to court: Michigan Legal Help has not automated such matters because they lack forms and may require narrative writing or briefing. She does not claim that AI can currently complete those proceedings or remove the need for legal support.

pts.k: Tripp predicts that adding AI to Michigan's follow-up messaging could make procedural support more flexible and easier to use.
pts.d: Ribadeneyra identifies a service gap after legal-aid organisations provide brief advice: clients may struggle to complete a multi-step process without further guidance or reminders. Tripp suggests AI could enhance Michigan Legal Help's What's Next text system, which currently uses a deliberately mapped logic tree and contains no AI. This is an exploratory proposal, not evidence that an AI-enabled reminder system has improved completion rates.

pts.k: Tripp warns that efficiency-oriented AI deployment in courts and agencies can harm litigants when tools are poorly understood, biased or insufficiently supervised.
pts.d: Tripp expects AI to increase speed and efficiency, but warns that these priorities can displace due process. Her concern is conditional on inadequate vetting, excessive trust, opaque inputs and missing human checks. She invokes Michigan's automated unemployment-fraud determinations as a concrete precedent for harmful automation, explicitly distinguishing that earlier algorithmic system from the AI tools under discussion. Her proposed safeguards include stakeholder involvement, transparency, education and human oversight; these are recommendations rather than demonstrated guarantees of safety.

pts.k: Ribadeneyra proposes using reliable statewide legal-help content to support more dependable AI-delivered information.
pts.d: Ribadeneyra asks whether a large language model could be trained on existing statewide legal-aid website content and deliver reliable resources to users. She expresses cautious optimism about near-term possibilities but offers this as a development idea, not an established capability or proof that restricting source content eliminates hallucinations. Her accompanying request for additional funding concerns equitable access to such technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists chiefly of implementation experience, named projects and an historical automation example; prospective benefits and market effects are not quantified.
pts.d: Tripp's strongest direct implementation evidence concerns staff drafting practices and Spot AI at Michigan Legal Help. Ribadeneyra draws on Technology Initiative Grant projects, including an unsuccessful Florida intake-document analysis project roughly four years earlier: the technology was not sufficiently mature to identify applicants' issues from uploaded documents. She also invokes GPT-4 passing the bar exam as a sign of changing capabilities, without providing benchmark details or claiming it establishes safe service delivery. The Michigan unemployment example supports Tripp's concern about unchecked automated decisions, not a measured generative-AI error rate. No controlled service-outcome studies, productivity estimates, comparative hallucination rates or cost analyses are supplied. Proposed case-management integrations and future narrative assistance remain proposals.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The discussion distinguishes current 2023 uses from near-term experiments and undated possibilities, with safe deployment dependent on checking, oversight and resources.
pts.d: Current uses include website drafting, broad issue classification, chatbots and AI embedded in commercial software. Tripp says Michigan Legal Help's updated website launched on May 1 and describes plans made eight months earlier as already overtaken by rapid change. Case-management assistance, AI-enhanced texting and content-grounded language models are prospective; help with matters lacking forms is qualified as something that may occur 'someday.' Neither speaker supplies a firm timetable for widespread adoption or closing the justice gap. Ribadeneyra stresses uncertainty even over the six-to-seven-month horizon leading to the January 2024 technology conference. Human review qualifies endorsed drafting uses, while funding and organisational capacity condition equitable adoption.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The central affected groups are low-income clients, self-represented litigants, legal-aid providers, courts and agencies, with large firms positioned as better-resourced adopters.
pts.d: Self-represented litigants could gain easier navigation, clearer information, drafting support and follow-up guidance, but face fabricated authorities and adverse automated decisions. Low-income benefits claimants are a concrete example of people exposed to administrative automation harms. Legal-aid attorneys could receive drafting, summarisation and issue-identification support while retaining human checking work; legal-help organisations also face responsibilities to monitor court and agency deployments. Courts and agencies are potential efficiency beneficiaries and decision-making risk sources. Larger firms and corporations are described as having resources to adopt tools unavailable to poorer users and providers. The episode does not make concrete predictions about lawyer headcount, associate staffing structures, billing models or displacement by alternative providers.
